tagline.text: A roughly 120 m waterfall hidden in the hills of Sigay, the tallest in the Ilocos Region

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Santo Rosario, Sigay, Ilocos Sur (via Tagudin)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1 night, 2 days (a day trip is tight)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,200–5,000 (round-trip bus from Manila, local transport and fees included, per person)

children.text: Aw-asen Falls drops roughly 120 m in the deep hill country of Sigay, Ilocos Sur, and is described as the tallest waterfall in the Ilocos Region. A hike of about 45 minutes past rice fields and two river crossings leads to a cold, clear basin below.
Aw-asen Falls is in Barangay Sto. Rosario in the municipality of Sigay, Ilocos Sur. Sigay is a landlocked mountain town on the edge of the Cordillera range, about
113 km
from coastal Vigan and about
343 km

from Manila, as reported by English Wikipedia (the straight-line distance on the map is shorter, about 60 km to Vigan and about 278 km to Manila). The Sigay local government and the Philippine Information Agency (PIA) both present the falls as the tallest in the Ilocos Region. The reported height varies by source. Most travel articles and trip reports say about
, while PIA gives about
, so it is safest to think of it as roughly 110–120 m. The English Wikipedia entry for Sigay lists 43 m (142 ft), which differs a lot from the other sources, so treat that figure with caution.

The water comes from a spring higher up and, because the area is remote, it is clear and unpolluted. The Sigay local government's page says locals drink it, and one trip report says it flows all year round. The name may be unfamiliar to many travelers, but the scenery is striking. A long ribbon of water pours down one wall of the gorge into a wide basin, and a large rock viewpoint facing the falls lets you take in the whole drop at once. Trip reports mention three viewpoints along the way: a side view from the trail, the popular rock viewpoint, and the base of the falls.

The journey is long, so a day trip from Manila is not realistic. From Manila, take a bus toward the Ilocos region and get off at Bitalag Junction in Tagudin, which usually takes 6 to 8 hours, then continue about
24 km
up a mountain road to Barangay Santo Rosario. The village sits at about

above sea level, so it feels cooler, and its registration area is the starting point for the hike. A realistic plan is to set aside one day of a northern Ilocos trip or to sleep a night in Vigan or Candon first.
The walk itself is not difficult. According to trip reports and guides, the trail is about
4 km
one way and mostly downhill, and the descent takes about
45 minutes

. Because the same trail is uphill on the way back, one source says an average traveler needs 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes to climb out. The route passes rice fields, crosses a hanging bridge, goes over the river twice, and then descends through forest steps. Hiring a local guide at the village is presented as a rule, and the guide decides whether the river crossings are safe based on the water level that day. Rules and fees change, so check with the Sigay tourism office before you go.

Known as the tallest waterfall in the Ilocos Region, it drops straight down a high gorge wall. Local tourism staff say the flow is bigger and more dramatic in the rainy season and continues through the dry season. The spray near the falls is strong, so keep cameras and belongings in a waterproof bag.

A large rock jutting out opposite the falls gives an unobstructed view of the whole waterfall, and it is a favorite spot for photos. If you go early in the morning there are fewer people, which also makes for better portraits. There are rest sheds along the steps down, so you can take breaks as you go.
The basin below the falls is very clear and cold, and the Sigay local government describes it as deep and still in summer. Only one guide gives a figure, about 7 feet (about
2 m

) deep, dropping off quickly from the edge, so treat it as a rough guide. Currents turn dangerous in the rainy season and are strong right under the falls, so only get in where your guide says it is safe.
You can cross the basin on a bamboo raft (balsa) to get closer to the falls. A village guide pulls the raft with a rope, and the fee is described as about
per person. The Sigay page notes that non-swimmers can ride it too.

From Santo Rosario you soon pass rice fields and cross a long metal hanging bridge. The bridge sways, but many trip reports say the view is as memorable as the falls. Sigay itself promotes its hanging bridges and terraced rice fields.

You cross the river twice along the trail, and one of the crossings has a hanging bridge. They can be dangerous after heavy rain, and the Sigay local government is reportedly building a bridge to replace the risky crossings, but no completion date has been announced. Your guide decides whether it is safe to cross.

Namengpengan Falls in Barangay Mabileg, Sigay, is visited together with Aw-asen on some group tours. Sangbay ni Ragsak Falls in neighboring Suyo is about 30 m high, with an easier trail and a shallow pool.

per group).
Walk down to the falls past rice fields and the hanging bridge, crossing the river on the way. It takes about
45 minutes
View the falls from the rock viewpoint, rest by the basin and take photos. Ride the bamboo raft if you like.
Climb back out, which takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes
, and eat your packed lunch at the village.
Stop at the Sigay town viewpoint (Tapawan View Deck), then continue to Candon or Vigan for the night.
Many trip reports recommend an early start to avoid crowds. In the rainy season you may meet rain on the way, so keep the afternoon schedule loose.
Leave Manila and spend time in Vigan. Walk along Calle Crisologo, have dinner and stay overnight.
Set out from Vigan or Tagudin junction and stop at the Tapawan View Deck in Sigay town on the way. One trip report says Sigay is about 2 hours from Vigan.
Hire a guide at the village registration area and walk to the falls and back.
Sigay is far from Vigan, so doing everything in one day is tight. Travel times depend on road conditions, so check locally.
From Cubao or Pasay in Manila, take a Partas, Viron or Dominion bus bound for Vigan or Laoag and get off at Bitalag Junction in Tagudin. It takes about
6–8 hours
Fares are described as about
for a regular bus and up to about
for a sleeper. They vary by company and season.
From Bitalag Junction to Santo Rosario, about
24 km
, take a monster jeepney (about
, though one source also mentions a scheduled ride at about
per person) or a round-trip habal-habal charter (about
). Drivers do not wait at the village entrance, so guides advise booking ahead with the Sigay tourism office.
Tagudin has bank ATMs, but Sigay does not. Bring enough cash in advance.
Search for Bitalag or Bitalag Satellite Market in your map app and drive via the NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX expressways. It takes about
5–6 hours
Past the junction the mountain road includes unpaved sections, so a regular sedan is not recommended. Use a monster jeepney or a 4x4 vehicle.
One source says it takes about
1.5 hours
from Candon City to Sigay, on mountain roads up to the town.
You can also start from Vigan, but Sigay is about
113 km
away, so leave early in the morning.
The nearest airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO), but it is far, so you must continue overland. Check routes and times with the airline.

The dry season from November to April is best. Trails are less slippery, the river crossings are safer and the basin is calmer. Some trip reports suggest going a few days after light rain, when the flow is strong and the water is clear.

In the rainy season the flow is bigger and more impressive, but the risk of flash floods rises and the trail turns muddy. The falls are said to flow year-round even in the dry season. Weekends and holidays are busier, so weekdays are better.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best time to trek, with clear water.
Easy trail conditions, but the midday heat is strong. A hat helps on the shadeless rice-field section.
Showers start to make the trail wet. On rainy days, check before heading in.
The flow is big, but river crossings and landslides are a serious risk.

There are no restaurants or shops near the falls, so bring packed food and water. Eateries in Tagudin town serve Ilocano dishes such as bagnet and pinakbet, and one trip report says you can taste local coffee in Sigay, a hill town known for growing coffee.

Lodging options include homestays in Sigay (arranged in advance with the local government), small inns in Tagudin and Candon, and hotels in Vigan. Camping near the falls must be coordinated with the Sigay tourism office, and overnight stays without permission are said not to be allowed.
Before your visit, contact the Sigay tourism office to book a monster jeepney and a guide. Contact numbers in trip reports can change, so confirm them on the Sigay local government website.
Aqua shoes or trekking sandals are comfortable because many parts are wet. Mossy rocks and wet steps are slippery.
There is no phone signal at the falls or on the trail. One trip report says a coin-operated Wi-Fi machine near the village registration area is available.
Starting early means fewer people and avoids the midday heat. Leave extra time for the climb back.
Put cameras and clothes in a waterproof bag because of the spray.
There are no trash bins, so carry all your trash out.
Bring enough drinking water, snacks and cash, and tell family about your plans.
If it is raining or it has rained upstream, the river crossings and the basin can become very dangerous, so follow your guide's judgment and do not push on.
The basin gets deep right from the edge and the current is said to be strong right under the falls, so do not swim directly beneath them.
Wet concrete steps and mossy rocks are slippery, so do not rush.
Flash floods can happen even when the trail looks clear.
Assume there are no shops, ATMs or clinics beyond Santo Rosario village and buy what you need beforehand.
Fees and rules differ between reports and change, so check the latest announcements.
